title: Partners, all
hookLine: all are partners in Your grace; You are outside no one (Majh M5, ang 97)

cards: Punjabi villages remember the sanjha chulha, a shared clay oven in the open. Women from different households brought their dough, sat together, slapped rotis onto the hot walls, and talked while the bread puffed.
Nobody owned the fire. Everybody used it. Sanjha means shared, held in common.
And Guru Arjan takes that everyday village word and uses it to describe the whole human race.

teach.b: The shabad is in Raag Majh, on ang 97. It opens, in effect: You are our common Master, our Father. Your storehouse holds the nine treasures, and it never runs out; whoever You give to is satisfied.
Then: all place their hope in You; You dwell in every heart.
All are called partners, saanjheevaal, in Your grace.

You are seen outside no one. Saanjheevaal is built from that same word, saanjh: a share, a partnership, the word for people who hold something together, like farmers who share a well or a team of oxen.
Guru Arjan says every person is a shareholder in the same grace. Not guests. Not customers.
Partners. A partner isn't someone you tolerate or help out of pity. A partner has an equal claim: the well is as much theirs as yours.
Then the second half: You are seen outside no one. In the hymn, there is no person in whom the One is absent. Put the two lines together and you have ground a lot of Sikh practice stands on.

Sikhs often point to lines like these to explain why langar feeds anyone, why the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar is known for doors on all four sides, open to all comers, and why the Ardas ends with good for all.
Not because everyone is the same; people are wildly different.
But because nobody is outside the partnership.
In the hymn's terms, the stranger in the next seat on the bus holds the same share in grace.

how: Sikhs sing Guru Arjan's Majh shabad of the common Master in kirtan; the line about all being partners is often cited for langar and for gurdwaras open to everyone.

o: sharers holding an equal claim to grace
customers buying a share of a farm
guests welcomed in out of kindness

p: the One is in every heart

s: saanjheevaal means guests who are allowed in
it means partners, with an equal share.
the hymn calls the One our common Master and Father
the hymn says some people are outside the One
You are seen outside no one.

games.q: a stranger sits down next to you at langar. in Guru Arjan's word, what are they?
o: a guest you're being kind to.
a partner with an equal share.
games.why: saanjheevaal: all are partners in the One's grace, and the One is outside no one.

practice: Bring to mind a stranger you'll probably see today, a bus driver, a cashier, a coworker you've never really talked to, and picture their face.

Hold Guru Arjan's word over them: partner, not a background extra in your day but a shareholder in the same grace, and notice if anything shifts in how you'd greet them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with their face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Partners. Saanjheevaal: in Guru Arjan's hymn, everyone holds an equal share in the One's grace, and the One is outside no one.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: partners, those who hold a share in common (modern spelling).

carryVoice: Your line: all partners. The well is as much theirs as yours. Day six hundred fifty-two, done.

sources.ref: Majh M5, Ang 97 (sabhe saanjheevaal sadaain, toon kisai na disahi baaharaa)
